A question that crosses several datasets

A solar eruption is observed near the Sun, while changes in solar wind and geomagnetic activity are measured at different locations and times. Investigating one event means aligning those views and keeping track of what each observation actually measures.

The public project brings observations, event selection, propagation calculations, and research notes into one interface. It supports moving from “what happened?” to “which assumptions explain this result?”

Observations with their context intact

The application combines NOAA solar-wind and magnetic-field products, Kp, GOES X-ray and proton data, and NASA DONKI event catalogs. A replay of 8–13 May 2024 connects the major storm’s solar-wind, magnetic, and geomagnetic records.

Time conventions, data provenance, and missing values remain visible. For example, time-shifted OMNI data are handled without adding the L1 propagation delay a second time, and gaps are not silently replaced with zero.

From a CME to an arrival-time estimate

The modeling view compares constant-speed propagation with an analytic Drag-Based Model. Adjusting the inputs makes the dependence on initial speed, background solar wind, and drag visible through arrival times and sensitivity analysis.

The 3D cone is a geometric representation built from event direction and angular width. It helps interpret the model, while the calculation itself is an analytic propagation estimate rather than a newly executed magnetohydrodynamic simulation.

Related work at SpaceData

At SpaceData, I built a Python application that ingests real-time NASA data, estimates CME arrival times, provides aurora forecasts, and displays the previous two weeks of data. I am also developing physics-based and time-series machine-learning models to investigate satellite and communications impacts.

The public repository linked here is the separate space-weather lab described above. Its source and public-data demonstrations should not be read as a release of SpaceData’s internal software, datasets, or commercial systems.

Making the model inspectable

The public app includes data-quality views, model checks, and account-specific research notes with Markdown export. Science tests cover reference arrival times, numerical derivatives, limiting cases, units, timestamps, and missing observations.

These tools support exploration and comparison with observations. A modeled CME arrival time does not by itself determine the strength of a geomagnetic storm; the interface keeps the measured quantities and model assumptions distinct.
